Find the approximate horizontal distance to an upright object whose height you know.
1. Enter the height between the object\'s top and bottom.
2. Keep the phone in the same spot. Tilt it to aim, without changing its position.
3. Aim the center reticle at the top, hold steady, and capture.
4. Aim at the bottom on the same vertical line. Hold steady and capture within 15 seconds.
5. Read the approximate horizontal distance. Use Restart to try again.
Use a vertical object and the correct height. Moving the phone or aiming off the same vertical line can spoil the result.
The result is approximate: accuracy is not calibrated and uncertainty is not quantified.
Think of two right triangles sharing the same horizontal distance d. At elevation θ, an endpoint is d × tan(θ) above the camera. Subtract the bottom offset from the top to get height H:

d — horizontal distance to the object's vertical line, in meters.
H — known vertical height between the endpoints, in meters.
θ (theta) — viewing angle above the horizontal plane. The subscripts top and bottom identify the endpoints; angles below horizontal are negative.
tan — tangent function; the calculation uses radians.
You get horizontal distance, not the sloping line-of-sight distance to either endpoint. The camera can be above or below the bottom; its height cancels when the offsets are subtracted.

Viewy combines phone orientation with a mapped rear-camera axis to find each viewing direction relative to gravity. Elevation is its angle above the horizontal plane, not simply phone pitch. Capture records the latest accepted sensor direction, not an averaged direction or a photo.

Both endpoints must share a horizontal position. Viewy checks their bearings and offers alignment guidance; near vertical, bearing is unreliable and capture is blocked. These checks cannot detect phone translation or prove the object is vertical.

Captures must share a sensor source, reference frame and camera mapping, with increasing sensor timestamps no more than 15 seconds apart. Interruptions clear incompatible captures. The preferred Game Rotation Vector can drift; the Rotation Vector fallback can respond to magnetic interference. The time limit does not bound drift or distance error.

When the two elevations nearly match, the denominator can be small. Small angle errors can then cause large distance errors. An incorrect height also scales the result directly. Viewy rejects insufficient separation and unusable geometry, but passing those checks does not guarantee accuracy.

The rear-camera axis uses suitable lens-pose metadata, or an uncalibrated rear-axis assumption when metadata is unavailable. Neither calibrates the center reticle. Lens distortion, focus, stabilization and camera processing can affect aiming.

The preview frame and sensor reading are not synchronized. Capture uses the latest accepted sensor direction, not the exposure time of the image you see. Hold still before and briefly after capturing to reduce motion effects; preview delays, especially in low light, remain unmeasured.

Readiness checks recent variation and freshness. A steady reading may still have sensor bias, slow drift or camera-axis error. Viewy does not turn steadiness or platform accuracy labels into an uncertainty interval.
Height equals horizontal distance times the difference between the tangents of the top and bottom elevation angles.
Horizontal distance equals height divided by the difference between the tangents of the top and bottom elevation angles.
